title: The Band of Holes

paragraphs.text: Archaeologist Charles Stanish of the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) is an expert on the ancient cultures of South America's Andes region. He is often contacted by members of the public, and one day he received a call from a man who had seen a TV programme claiming that aliens played a large role in the lives of ancient people. This man was interested in getting Stanish's opinion on a strange arrangement of pits in the ground known as the Band of Holes. Located on a hill called Monte Sierpe within Peru's Pisco Valley, the holes had supposedly been created by extraterrestrials according to the TV programme. Stanish had never heard of the site, although he had worked in the area for more than 30 years. He and his colleague Henry Tantalean then took a look at the satellite imagery of the Band of Holes, and were surprised to see what was indeed an extraordinary artificial feature. 'I'd never seen anything like it,' says Stanish. Intrigued, they decided to investigate the curious site.

Stanish and Tantalean conducted a survey which showed that most of the holes were about a metre across and 50 to 100 centimetres deep. The two archaeologists also noted that they were divided into several unique groupings, which they called blocks, each of which had irregular patterns of holes. Using a drone, they collected aerial images and created a new, detailed map of the Band of Holes, which they estimated consisted of between 5,000 and 6,000 depressions. After surveying and studying the site, they found not only the remains of an Inca road nearby, but also a series of Inca-colcas, Inca-period storage houses. Together with the discovery of Inca-period storage houses. Together with the discovery of Inca-period pottery near the band, these finds seemed to confirm Stanish and Tantalean's initial instinct that the Band of Holes dated to some time around the fifteenth century. This period was after the Inca Empire conquered the Chincha people, who were native to the region. Stanish and Tantalean also the holes were once used to store something, but just what and why still wasn't clear. Back at UCLA, Stanish attended a lecture given by Peruvian archaeologist Alejandro Chu about recent discoveries at the Inca site of Inkawasi, about 120 kilometres north of Monte Sterpe. In colcas at this site, Chu had found a number of Inca-period objects known as khipus. These were used to keep a note of goods that local farmers laid on the storage house floor, which was divided into squares like a checkerboard.

Stanish was impressed by Chu's lecture, and immediately saw a similarity between the Inkawasi checkerboard and the layout of the Band of Holes. The rest of the puzzle then began to fall into place. Stanish notes that Monte Sterpe is only six kilometres from Tambo Colorado, a massive 15th-century Inca administrative centre built above the agriculturally productive Pisco Valley. The Band of Holes is constructed along a road leading from the valley floor to Tambo Colorado. 'It's the perfect place to measure your produce,' says Stanish. His theory is that Pisco Valley farmers brought crops to the Band of Holes as a form of tax and that each family or social group placed chilis or other farming produce into the holes in front of the state's accountants. The accountants would probably have used khipus (essentially strings with a series of knots on them) to keep a record. The goods could have then been transported to Tambo Colorado, or wherever else the authorities wanted to take them.

Stanish will need to come up with hard evidence to convince his fellow scholars. Jean-Pierre Protzen, a specialist in Inca architecture at the University of California, Berkeley has his own theories about Monte Sterpe. Protzen has spent years working at Tambo Colorado, and feels the Band of Holes does not date from the same time as the massive Inca centre. He thinks the holes may have been used to store guano, a substance produced by birds, which was widely used to fertilise crops. 'It's amazing visually,' says Protzen of the site, 'but we still don' t know much about it.’

Stanish agrees that his hypothesis needs to be tested. 'Sure, it's speculative,' he says. 'But we could be on the cusp of a whole new understanding of Inca accounting.' He points out that other sites in the area with unusual alignments that have traditionally been considered religious might also have had roles in administering the tax-collecting system. 'If I'm right, then we're going to have to think differently about a lot of sites that have been regarded as strictly ritual,' says Stanish.
